intro: A bassoon reaches for a high C; a few minutes later, the strings stamp on a chord that seems to bruise the floor. Stravinsky conducts the Columbia Symphony Orchestra in this 1960 recording of his pagan spring.

sections.label: Intro · The high bassoon
sections.mNote: A lone melody grows into a thicket of woodwind

sections.label: A · Augurs of Spring
sections.mNote: Strings stamp; horns move the accents

sections.label: B · Ritual of Abduction
sections.mNote: Running strings and sharp wind cries

sections.label: C · Spring Rounds
sections.mNote: Two clarinets sing before the heavy dance

sections.label: D · Ritual of the Rival Tribes
sections.mNote: Low brass confronts quick, high figures

sections.label: E · Procession of the Sage
sections.mNote: Tubas and horns march through the crowd

sections.label: Link · The Sage kisses the earth
sections.mNote: Low winds, a quiet bass and held strings

sections.label: F · Dance of the Earth
sections.mNote: Bass drum and rushing strings break the stillness

cues.title: The bassoon’s high C
cues.text: The bassoon begins high in its range, bending a little melody around C. Its soft, pinched voice has the stage to itself. Other winds gradually find their way in, each with a phrase of its own; the spring landscape fills with calls.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 1–4, opening and rehearsal figures 1–4: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The woman in squirrel fur
cues.text: Writing to the painter Nicholas Roerich on 26 September 1911, Stravinsky says: “The picture of the old woman in a squirrel fur sticks in my mind.” He imagines her running before the dancers, stopping them, breaking into their rhythm. The ballet is already moving in his head.
cues.evidence: Stravinsky to Nicholas Roerich, 26 September 1911, on composing the Augurs of Spring; translated in Pieter C. van den Toorn, Stravinsky and The Rite of Spring (1987), pp. 3–4: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: One chord, uneven blows
cues.text: The strings repeat a chord made by pressing F♭ major against an E♭ dominant seventh. Horns strike selected notes harder. The written bars stay in two beats, yet the accents keep landing somewhere else: the dancers have a floor, and it keeps jolting under them.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 12–14, rehearsal figure 13: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, chapter 3, examples 15–18, analyses the chord and its accents in 2/4: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The abduction breaks loose
cues.text: Presto: the violins run, high winds cry out in short bursts, and the horns hold notes through the commotion. A phrase gets just enough time to show its face before another shoulders it aside. The dance feels crowded with bodies.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 32–34, rehearsal figure 37 and the opening of the Ritual of Abduction: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two clarinets, far apart
cues.text: The little E♭ clarinet and the bass clarinet sing the same tune in octaves beneath trilling flutes. Then the strings begin their broad, heavy tread. Stravinsky writes Sostenuto e pesante: the round dance carries its weight on every step.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 45–47, rehearsal figures 48–49, Tranquillo followed by Sostenuto e pesante: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A ballroom in Brooklyn
cues.text: This orchestra assembles in the ballroom of Brooklyn’s St George Hotel on 5 and 6 January 1960. The composer stands at the podium. The music that once accompanied Nijinsky’s stamping dancers now fills a hotel ballroom for Columbia’s microphones.
cues.evidence: Parnassus PACL 95003/4 booklet, p. 2, gives the performers, venue and session dates: https://media.musicalconcepts.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/28214506/PACL-95003_4-Booklet.pdf. Van den Toorn, pp. 1–6, describes the original ballet and Nijinsky’s choreography: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: The tribes answer back
cues.text: Trombones and tubas put down a heavy phrase. Faster figures answer higher up. Soon the two are sounding together: the low music holds its ground while the upper parts rush across it. The rivalry is written into the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 54–55, rehearsal figure 57: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, pp. 19–20, describes the two groups and their combination five bars into rehearsal figure 57: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tubas keep coming
cues.text: The tubas repeat their lumbering tune while horns insist on a different pattern. Bassoons and low strings keep moving underneath. The phrases have unequal lengths, so their meeting points shift as the Sage’s procession pushes forward.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 65–73, rehearsal figures 64–70: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, p. 19, discusses the overlapping cycles in the procession: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A kiss on the ground
cues.text: The Sage bends to kiss the earth. Bassoons and contrabassoon murmur over quiet timpani and a low bass; the strings hold a faint, strange chord. After all those feet and horns, the ceremony has almost nothing left to say aloud.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 74, rehearsal figure 71, Lento: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. The ballet scenario describes the Sage’s kiss: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The earth breaks loose
cues.text: The bass drum starts the next dance. Winds and strings sweep upwards, and the whole orchestra hurls itself into repeated figures. Prestissimo is the marking. The Sage’s brief stillness gives way to a dance with scarcely room for a breath.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 74–85, rehearsal figure 72 to the end of Part I: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The strings plant their feet
transitions.how: The bassoon’s opening phrase returns as the other wind voices fall away. Plucked violins begin a short repeating figure. At Tempo giusto, second violins, violas, cellos and basses stamp the F♭-major/E♭-seventh chord; horns pick out the irregular accents. The wandering introduction has acquired a hard floor.

transitions.title: The violins start running
transitions.how: The heavy end of the Augurs breaks into Presto. Running violin figures and short high-wind calls cut across held horn notes; low strings supply sharply repeated attacks. The sudden quicker pace sends the dancers scattering before the earlier stamping has time to settle.

transitions.title: Clarinets sing under trilling flutes
transitions.how: The fast dance stops. At Tranquillo, flutes trill while E♭ clarinet and bass clarinet sing in octaves; brass and strings are silent. The bass clarinet is now the lowest voice. This little wind choir opens the door to the slower, heavy string chords of Sostenuto e pesante.

transitions.title: Low brass answers the quiet
transitions.to: D · Ritual of the Rival Tribes
transitions.how: The round dance ends with its quiet flute-and-clarinet music. Molto allegro brings in trombones and tubas, answered by bassoons and horns. Low strings reinforce the tread. Within a few bars, quick high figures break across the heavy phrase: the two tribes have met.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 53–55, rehearsal figures 56–57: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, p. 19: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

transitions.title: The procession is already approaching
transitions.from: D · Ritual of the Rival Tribes
transitions.how: The tuba tune begins before the printed procession heading. By the time the Sage arrives, it is repeating over bassoon and low-string figures, with horns carrying their own pattern above it. The march grows out of the crowd; its phrases keep their separate lengths as more players join.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 65–73, rehearsal figures 64–70: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, p. 19, places the tuba entrance at 64 and the procession heading at 67: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

transitions.title: The procession falls silent
transitions.to: Link · The Sage kisses the earth
transitions.how: The crowded procession falls away into Lento. Bassoons and contrabassoon repeat their low notes over quiet timpani and a solo bass. The strings then hold a hushed chord, coloured by harmonics. The Sage touches the ground in this sudden clearing.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 74, rehearsal figure 71 and the held chord before 72: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf

transitions.title: The bass drum breaks in
transitions.from: Link · The Sage kisses the earth
transitions.how: The string chord hangs under a pause. A bass-drum roll begins Prestissimo; horns and trumpets enter, followed by an upward rush through winds and strings. The low drum keeps sounding beneath the new figures. The ceremony’s stillest moment opens straight into its fastest dance.

source.title: Stravinsky, The Rite of Spring, full score, Dover reprint of corrected Boosey text
source.locator: Part I, pp. 1–85; opening and rehearsals 13, 37, 48–49, 57, 67, 71–72. Approximate passage states, not attack-level alignment. The later corrected print is used only for these shared scoring features; the different 1943 finale heard in Part II is not mapped from this score.

timeline.note: The opening centres on the high bassoon melody with sparse horn support; other reeds join as the introduction unfolds.
The early introduction interweaves reed strands with sparse horn support; this snapshot does not identify a string entrance.
The first Augurs block repeats a string chord; horns reinforce selected attacks. First violins are absent from this opening block.
The abduction ritual combines moving strings and short high-wind gestures with brass and percussion support.
The quiet frame of Spring Rounds places its melody in small and bass clarinets against sustained flutes.
The heavy round dance adds repeated lower-wind and string chords beneath a broad melodic line.
Low brass opens the rival-tribes exchange; horn and bassoon figures answer before the higher orchestral block.
The procession overlaps recurring tuba and horn figures with lower strings and reeds.
Low winds and a quiet bass support the Sage’s brief stillness; a held string chord precedes the restart.
The Dance of the Earth launches rapid sweeps and repeated massed patterns after the held chord.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: He could make a roomful of dancers lose their footing with one displaced accent, then write a psalm that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
In St Petersburg, opera was the family business. Stravinsky’s father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. Born in 1882 at Oranienbaum, he entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks showed what he could do with an orchestra in a few minutes. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. Then came a whole ballet, The Firebird. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he remembered the rehearsals ending with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
